questions.stem: The Companies Act 2013 extends to:

readLink.label: Read: Where the Act applies — s.1 →

options.text: The whole of India except the State of Jammu and Kashmir
options.explanation: That exception belonged to older Central legislation; the 2013 Act's extent clause carries no such exclusion today.

options.text: The whole of India except the Scheduled Areas
options.explanation: Scheduled Areas are a Constitutional concept about legislative administration; they do not limit the Act's extent.

options.text: The whole of India
options.explanation: s.1(2) states the extent in exactly these words — there is no State carve-out left in the Act.

options.text: Companies registered in India and their branches abroad only
options.explanation: This confuses extent (the territory the statute covers) with the reach of particular provisions over foreign operations.

questions.stem: A banking company incorporated under the Companies Act 2013 contends that the Act does not apply to it because it is governed by the Banking Regulation Act 1949. The correct position is:

readLink.label: Read: Where the Act applies — s.1 →

options.text: The Companies Act applies to it, except in so far as its provisions are inconsistent with the Banking Regulation Act 1949
options.explanation: s.1(4) carves banking companies IN, subject to the sectoral statute prevailing only to the extent of an inconsistency.

options.text: The Companies Act does not apply to banking companies at all
options.explanation: This reads the sectoral saving as a total exclusion; s.1(4)(c) expressly applies the Act to banking companies.

options.text: The Companies Act applies only to those banking companies that are listed
options.explanation: Listing is irrelevant to s.1(4); the carve-in is by activity, not by listing status.

options.text: The Banking Regulation Act applies only where the Companies Act is silent
options.explanation: That reverses the rule — the special Act prevails over an inconsistent Companies Act provision, not merely where the Act says nothing.

questions.stem: A company incorporated in 1974 under the Companies Act 1956 and still carrying on business is today governed by:

readLink.label: Read: Where the Act applies — s.1 →

options.text: The Companies Act 1956, which continues to govern companies formed under it
options.explanation: The 1956 Act has been repealed; existing companies were carried over into the 2013 Act, not left behind under the old one.

options.text: The Companies Act 2013 only after it re-registers itself under that Act
options.explanation: No re-registration is required — s.1(4)(a) applies the Act to such companies directly.

options.text: Both Acts equally, with the earlier Act prevailing on conflict
options.explanation: There is no such dual regime; the sectoral-override idea of s.1(4) applies to special Acts, not to the repealed 1956 Act.

options.text: The Companies Act 2013, which applies to companies incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law
options.explanation: s.1(4)(a) reaches companies formed under any previous company law, and s.2(20) treats them as companies for the Act.

questions.stem: Under s.2(20), 'company' means a company incorporated:

readLink.label: Read: Company and body corporate — ss.2(20), 2(11) →

options.text: Under any law in force in India that confers corporate personality
options.explanation: This is the test for a body corporate under s.2(11), not for a company under s.2(20).

options.text: Under the Companies Act 2013 or under any previous company law
options.explanation: That is the whole of the definition — incorporation under the company-law statute is the only qualifying route.

options.text: Under the Companies Act 2013 only
options.explanation: It omits the second limb; companies formed under earlier company law are equally companies under s.2(20).

options.text: Under the Companies Act 2013 or the Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008
options.explanation: An LLP is a body corporate under its own Act, but it is never a 'company' for s.2(20).

questions.stem: Which of the following is expressly EXCLUDED from the definition of 'body corporate' in s.2(11)?

readLink.label: Read: Company and body corporate — ss.2(20), 2(11) →

options.text: A company incorporated outside India
options.explanation: The definition expressly INCLUDES a company incorporated outside India — this option inverts the clause.

options.text: A co-operative society registered under a law relating to co-operative societies
options.explanation: s.2(11) excludes co-operative societies, and any other body corporate notified by the Central Government.

options.text: A limited liability partnership
options.explanation: An LLP has corporate personality and is a body corporate; the exclusions listed in s.2(11) do not cover it.

options.text: A company registered under section 8
options.explanation: A s.8 company is a company, and therefore a body corporate; the exclusion list does not mention it.

questions.stem: Trentmoor plc, incorporated in the United Kingdom, has a branch office in Chennai. For the Companies Act 2013 it is:

readLink.label: Read: Company and body corporate — ss.2(20), 2(11) →

options.text: A company under s.2(20), because it carries on business in India
options.explanation: Carrying on business in India does not create incorporation in India — s.2(20) turns on the place of incorporation only.

options.text: Neither a company nor a body corporate, being incorporated abroad
options.explanation: This misses the express inclusion of foreign-incorporated companies in s.2(11).

options.text: A body corporate only if the Central Government notifies it as such
options.explanation: The notification power in s.2(11) is used to EXCLUDE bodies corporate, not to admit them.

options.text: A body corporate, and (if it also conducts business activity in India) a foreign company — but not a 'company' under s.2(20)
options.explanation: s.2(11) includes a company incorporated outside India within 'body corporate'; s.2(20) is confined to Indian incorporation; s.2(42) then labels it a foreign company.

questions.stem: The proposition that a company is a legal person distinct from its members, so that a controlling member who lends to the company on security ranks as a secured creditor, is anchored in:
questions.sourceRef: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd (1897)

readLink.label: Read: Features that follow from incorporation →

options.text: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd
options.explanation: Salomon settled that a duly incorporated company is a separate person, whatever the concentration of ownership behind it.

options.text: Daimler Co Ltd v Continental Tyre & Rubber Co
options.explanation: Daimler is the enemy-character case — it lifted the veil in wartime; it is not the authority for the separate-entity rule.

options.text: Jones v Lipman
options.explanation: Jones v Lipman pierced the veil where a company was used as a mask to defeat a contract of sale.

options.text: Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd
options.explanation: That case ignored a subsidiary created to depress a bonus entitlement — again a piercing case, not the founding rule.

questions.stem: Every one of the five members of Kalanjali Private Limited dies in the same accident. The company:

readLink.label: Read: Features that follow from incorporation →

options.text: Stands automatically dissolved for want of members
options.explanation: Death of members does not dissolve a company; only winding up or striking off ends its existence.

options.text: Must be wound up within six months unless new members are admitted
options.explanation: This mixes up perpetual succession with s.3A, which imposes personal liability (not dissolution) when membership falls below the statutory minimum for over six months.

options.text: Continues in existence; the shares devolve on the legal representatives and the company is unaffected in law
options.explanation: Perpetual succession means the company's existence is independent of changes in, or the death of, its members.

options.text: Continues, but its existing contracts lapse until new members are admitted
options.explanation: Contracts are the company's own; they are unaffected by a change in the persons who hold its shares.

questions.stem: Following the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015, the common seal:
questions.sourceRef: Companies (Amendment) Act 2015 — common seal made optional

readLink.label: Read: Features that follow from incorporation →

options.text: Is optional; where a company has none, the relevant documents are signed by two directors, or by one director and the company secretary where one is appointed
options.explanation: The 2015 amendment made the seal optional and supplied the signing alternative, so the seal is no longer a defining feature of a company.

options.text: Remains compulsory for every company incorporated in India
options.explanation: This ignores the 2015 amendment entirely — the seal ceased to be mandatory.

options.text: Is optional for private companies but compulsory for public companies
options.explanation: The relaxation is not split by class of company; it applies to companies generally.

options.text: Was abolished, so no company may now use a common seal
options.explanation: Optional is not abolished — a company may still adopt and use a seal if it wishes.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · Separate entity · Member as employee
questions.stem: A person is the controlling shareholder and sole working director of a company and is also employed by it under a contract of service. On his death in the course of that employment his widow claims employment-related compensation. On the separate-entity principle:

readLink.label: Read: Features that follow from incorporation →

options.text: The claim fails — a person cannot contract with himself
options.explanation: The premise is wrong: the contract is between the individual and the company, which is a different person in law.

options.text: The claim fails unless the veil is lifted to reveal the true employer
options.explanation: Lifting would defeat the claim, not support it; the claim succeeds precisely because the veil stays in place.

options.text: The claim stands — the company and the individual are distinct persons, so a controlling member can validly be an employee of his own company
options.explanation: This is the proposition in Lee v Lee's Air Farming: the contract was between two separate legal persons and remained a contract of service.

options.text: The claim stands only if the individual held less than a majority of the shares
options.explanation: The size of the holding is irrelevant to separate personality — that was the point of Salomon.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a requirement that the articles of a private company must contain under s.2(68)?

options.text: A restriction on the right to transfer its shares
options.explanation: This is limb (i) of s.2(68) and is required.

options.text: A prohibition on the transfer of shares
options.explanation: The articles must RESTRICT the right to transfer, which means regulate it (pre-emption, board refusal) — an outright prohibition is not what the clause requires.

options.text: A limit of 200 on the number of members, except in the case of a One Person Company
options.explanation: This is limb (ii) and is required, with the OPC carve-out written into the clause.

options.text: A prohibition on any invitation to the public to subscribe for its securities
options.explanation: This is limb (iii) and is required.

questions.stem: The minimum paid-up share capital required of a private company as the law stands on 28 February 2026 is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(68) as amended by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015

options.explanation: That was the figure in the clause as originally enacted; it was omitted by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2015.
₹5 lakh was the old floor for a PUBLIC company, and it too was omitted in 2015.
₹4 crore is the small-company paid-up capital CEILING under the Rules — a ceiling for an exemption, not a floor for incorporation.

options.text: Nil — the ₹1 lakh figure was omitted in 2015 and no amount stands prescribed
options.explanation: The clause now reads 'such minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed', and nothing has been prescribed, so there is no floor.

questions.stem: The register of Tara Weaves Private Limited shows: 176 persons holding shares in their own names; 9 shareholdings each held jointly by 4 persons; 31 current employees of the company who hold shares; and 12 former employees who became members while in employment and have continued as members since leaving. For the purposes of s.2(68)(ii), the number of members is:

options.explanation: This counts the 36 joint holders individually (176 + 36) instead of treating each joint holding as one member.
This adds the 31 employee-members and the 12 continuing ex-employee members, both of which the second proviso excludes.
This counts joint holders individually AND includes employee and ex-employee members — both provisos ignored.
176 individual members + 9 (each joint holding of 4 counts as ONE member) = 185; current and continuing ex-employee members are excluded by the second proviso.

questions.stem: Mr Iyer worked for Sundara Mills Private Limited for eleven years, resigned in 2023, and bought 500 shares in the company in 2025. For the 200-member cap he:

options.text: Is excluded — he is a former employee of the company
options.explanation: Being a former employee is not enough; the clause requires membership to have begun during the employment.

options.text: Counts as a member — the exclusion needs him to have BECOME a member while in the employment of the company
options.explanation: Proviso (B) protects only a person who was a member while employed and continued as one after leaving; acquiring shares after resignation fails that condition.

options.text: Is excluded — any person who has ever been an employee is outside the count
options.explanation: This drops both the 'member while in that employment' and the 'continued to be a member' conditions.

options.text: Counts as half a member, being a part-period member
options.explanation: There is no fractional counting anywhere in s.2(68); the only aggregation rule is the joint-holder proviso.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(68)(ii) · Headroom in the cap
questions.stem: Vyoma Ceramics Private Limited has on its register 154 individual members, 8 shareholdings each held jointly by 2 persons, and 22 current employees of the company who hold shares. Ignoring any other change, the number of ADDITIONAL members (none of them employees or joint holders) the company may admit without breaching s.2(68)(ii) is:

options.explanation: This counts the 16 joint holders individually (154 + 16 = 170), leaving headroom of 30 instead of 38.
This includes the 22 employee-members in the count (154 + 8 + 22 = 184), which the second proviso excludes.
Counted members = 154 + 8 (each joint holding is one member) = 162; employee-members are excluded; 200 − 162 = 38.
This counts joint holders individually AND includes the employee-members (154 + 16 + 22 = 192).

questions.stem: Meghdoot Systems Private Limited is incorporated on 12 February 2026. Its first financial year under s.2(41) ends on:

options.text: 31 March 2027
options.explanation: A company incorporated on or after 1 January takes its first financial year to the 31 March of the FOLLOWING year — here a period of about fourteen months.

options.text: 31 March 2026
options.explanation: That would apply had the company been incorporated before 1 January; the clause pushes an on-or-after-1-January incorporation to the next 31 March.

options.text: 11 February 2027
options.explanation: s.2(41) does not permit an anniversary year-end; the financial year of a company always ends on 31 March, subject only to the proviso.

options.text: 31 December 2026
options.explanation: A calendar year-end is available only under the proviso, on an application by a company connected to a foreign company for consolidation purposes.

questions.stem: Under s.2(71), a public company is a company which:

options.text: Has its securities listed on a recognised stock exchange
options.explanation: That is the listed-company definition in s.2(52); listing is not what makes a company public.

options.text: Has at least seven members and a paid-up capital of ₹5,00,000
options.explanation: Seven is the minimum number of subscribers under s.3 for incorporation, and the ₹5 lakh floor was omitted in 2015; neither is the definition.

options.text: Is not a private company and has such minimum paid-up share capital as may be prescribed
options.explanation: The clause is framed negatively — anything that is not a private company is a public company — with a prescribed-capital limb that currently prescribes nothing.

options.text: Invites the public to subscribe for its securities
options.explanation: A public company MAY do so, but a public company that never makes a public offer is still a public company.

questions.stem: Sunbeam Logistics Private Limited, whose articles contain all three private-company restrictions and which has 41 members, is a subsidiary of Harita Ventures Limited, an unlisted public company. Sunbeam is:

options.text: A private company, because its articles contain all three restrictions
options.explanation: The proviso operates in spite of the articles — that is precisely what 'even where such subsidiary company continues to be a private company in its articles' means.

options.text: A private company, because it has fewer than 200 members
options.explanation: The member count is irrelevant to the deeming; the identity of the holding company is the only trigger.

options.text: A public company only if it alters its articles and changes its name
options.explanation: The deeming is automatic and needs no alteration; the company keeps its articles and its 'Private Limited' name.

options.text: A public company for the purposes of the Act, notwithstanding its articles and its name
options.explanation: The proviso deems a subsidiary of a company that is not a private company to be a public company, even where the subsidiary continues to be private in its articles.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(71) proviso · Limits of the deeming
questions.stem: Kadamba Traders Private Limited holds 80% of the voting power of Nilaya Foods Private Limited. Nilaya's articles carry all three private-company restrictions. Nilaya is:

options.text: A private company — the deeming applies only where the holding company is NOT a private company
options.explanation: The proviso is triggered by a subsidiary 'of a company, not being a private company'. A private parent does not trigger it.

options.text: A public company, because it is the subsidiary of another company
options.explanation: Being a subsidiary is not enough; the parent must itself be a non-private company.

options.text: A public company, because 80% exceeds three-fourths of the voting power
options.explanation: There is no three-fourths test in s.2(71) or s.2(87); the relevant threshold for subsidiary status is more than one-half.

options.text: A private company only until its members exceed 50
options.explanation: The private-company member cap is 200, and in any event the cap has nothing to do with the deeming proviso.

questions.stem: Under s.2(62), a One Person Company means a company which:

options.text: Has only one director
options.explanation: One director is the minimum an OPC may have, but the definition is framed by membership, not by the size of the Board.

options.text: Has only one person as a member
options.explanation: That is the whole of s.2(62); the OPC is then formed as a private company, with a nominee named in the memorandum.

options.text: Has one member and one nominee, both of whom are members
options.explanation: The nominee is not a member; the nominee becomes one only on the subscriber's death or incapacity to contract.

options.text: Is owned by a single body corporate
options.explanation: The definition speaks of one PERSON as a member, and the incorporation Rules confine OPC membership to natural persons.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(62) · Classification of an OPC
questions.stem: Which statement about a One Person Company is CORRECT?

options.text: It is a third class of company, distinct from private and public companies
options.explanation: The Act treats the OPC as a private company, not as a separate class alongside private and public.

options.text: It is a private company, the 200-member limb of s.2(68) is expressly disapplied to it, and it can also be a small company if it meets the s.2(85) tests
options.explanation: The OPC is a species of private company; s.2(68)(ii) opens with 'except in case of One Person Company'; and nothing in s.2(85) excludes an OPC.

options.text: It can never be a small company, because it has only one member
options.explanation: s.2(85) turns on capital, turnover and the three exclusions — the number of members is irrelevant to it.

options.text: It is a public company if its paid-up capital exceeds ₹50 lakh
options.explanation: That figure came from the old OPC conversion Rules, which were omitted in 2021; it never converted an OPC into a public company in any case.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(85) · Structure of the test
questions.stem: The two quantitative limbs of the small-company definition in s.2(85) are applied:

options.text: Cumulatively — paid-up capital AND turnover of the immediately preceding financial year must both be within the prescribed limits
options.explanation: The clause joins the two limbs with 'and'; failing either one takes the company out of the definition.

options.text: Alternatively — satisfying either limb is enough
options.explanation: This reads 'and' as 'or'; a company inside the capital limit but over the turnover limit is not small.

options.text: Cumulatively, but turnover is measured for the current financial year
options.explanation: The clause expressly uses the turnover as per the profit and loss account for the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING financial year.

options.text: Cumulatively, with turnover measured as an average of the last three financial years
options.explanation: There is no averaging in s.2(85); a single preceding-year figure is used.

questions.stem: On the position as on 28 February 2026, which of the following is a SMALL company?
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(85) with the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules

options.text: Bellary Tools Private Limited — paid-up capital ₹1.20 crore, preceding-year turnover ₹47 crore, no exclusion applies
options.explanation: The turnover limb fails: ₹47 crore exceeds the prescribed ₹40 crore, and both limbs must be satisfied.

options.text: Chandra Poly Private Limited — paid-up capital ₹0.50 crore, preceding-year turnover ₹6 crore, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Deccan Ltd
options.explanation: A subsidiary is excluded outright by proviso (A), however small its capital and turnover.

options.text: Everest Textiles Limited — an unlisted public company with paid-up capital ₹1 crore and preceding-year turnover ₹5 crore
options.explanation: The clause opens 'other than a public company'; a public company can never be small, listed or not.

options.text: Amrut Foods Private Limited — paid-up capital ₹3.60 crore, preceding-year turnover ₹36 crore, no exclusion applies
options.explanation: Both limbs are within the prescribed ₹4 crore and ₹40 crore, and none of the three exclusions applies.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the exclusions written into s.2(85)?

options.text: A holding company or a subsidiary company
options.explanation: This is exclusion (A) and applies however small the company's capital and turnover are.

options.text: A company registered under section 8
options.explanation: This is exclusion (B).

options.text: A One Person Company
options.explanation: The proviso excludes only a holding or subsidiary company, a s.8 company, and a company or body corporate governed by a special Act — an OPC is not excluded.

options.text: A company or body corporate governed by any special Act
options.explanation: This is exclusion (C) — the same phrase that appears in s.1(4), doing a different job there.

questions.stem: Neelkanth Alloys Private Limited has paid-up share capital of exactly ₹4,00,00,000 and turnover for the immediately preceding financial year of exactly ₹40,00,00,000. It is not a holding or subsidiary company, is not registered under s.8, and is not governed by any special Act. On the position as on 28 February 2026 it is:

options.text: A small company — both limbs use 'does not exceed', so a figure equal to the limit is within it
options.explanation: Capital ₹4 crore is not more than ₹4 crore and turnover ₹40 crore is not more than ₹40 crore; no exclusion applies.

options.text: Not a small company, because the paid-up capital equals the prescribed limit
options.explanation: The clause says 'does not exceed'; a figure equal to the limit is within it.

options.text: Not a small company, because the turnover equals the prescribed limit
options.explanation: Same misreading on the second limb — equality is not excess.

options.text: Not a small company, because both figures are at the prescribed limits and the clause requires a margin
options.explanation: s.2(85) prescribes no margin; the comparator is simply 'does not exceed'.

questions.stem: Sahyadri Infra Limited has paid-up share capital of ₹50 crore, of which the Central Government holds ₹14 crore, the Government of Maharashtra ₹9 crore and the Government of Karnataka ₹3 crore; the balance is held by the public. The aggregate Government holding and the company's status are:

readLink.label: Read: Government, foreign and listed companies →

options.text: 28% — not a Government company
options.explanation: This takes the Central Government's holding alone; s.2(45) expressly allows Central and State holdings to be combined.

options.text: 46% — not a Government company
options.explanation: This drops the Karnataka holding; every Government holding, Central or State, enters the aggregate.

options.text: 52% — not a Government company, because no single Government holds 51%
options.explanation: There is no single-Government requirement; the clause covers holdings 'partly by the Central Government and partly by one or more State Governments'.

options.text: 52% — a Government company
options.explanation: Central ₹14 crore + Maharashtra ₹9 crore + Karnataka ₹3 crore = ₹26 crore of ₹50 crore = 52%, which is not less than 51%, and s.2(45) aggregates Central and State holdings.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(45) · Subsidiary of a Government company
questions.stem: Bharat Heavy Systems Ltd is a Government company. Its wholly-owned subsidiary, Bharat Rail Components Ltd, has no direct Government shareholding at all. Bharat Rail Components Ltd is:

readLink.label: Read: Government, foreign and listed companies →

options.text: Not a Government company, because no Government holds 51% of its capital directly
options.explanation: This applies only the first limb of s.2(45) and ignores the express inclusion of subsidiaries.

options.text: A Government company only if the Central Government notifies it as such
options.explanation: No notification is needed; the inclusion operates by force of the definition.

options.text: A Government company, because the definition expressly INCLUDES a subsidiary of a Government company
options.explanation: The inclusion in the closing words of s.2(45) covers a subsidiary of a Government company regardless of direct Government shareholding.

options.text: Deemed a Government company in the same way a subsidiary of a public company is deemed public
options.explanation: The mechanism is different: s.2(45) INCLUDES subsidiaries in the definition, whereas s.2(71) uses a deeming proviso — and mixing the two is a marks-losing slip.

questions.stem: Under s.2(42), a company or body corporate incorporated outside India is a foreign company where it:

readLink.label: Read: Government, foreign and listed companies →

options.text: Has a place of business in India OR conducts any business activity in India
options.explanation: This reads 'and' as 'or' — the commonest misreading of s.2(42).

options.text: Has a place of business in India, whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, AND conducts any business activity in India in any other manner
options.explanation: The clause joins the two limbs with 'and'; a place of business alone, or activity alone, does not answer the definition.

options.text: Has any Indian shareholder holding not less than 20% of its capital
options.explanation: Shareholding is irrelevant to s.2(42); the test is presence plus activity in India.

options.text: Is incorporated outside India, whatever its activities
options.explanation: Foreign incorporation alone makes it a body corporate under s.2(11), not a foreign company under s.2(42).

questions.stem: Under the main limb of s.2(52), a listed company is one which has:

readLink.label: Read: Government, foreign and listed companies →

options.text: Its equity shares listed on any recognised stock exchange
options.explanation: This narrows 'any of its securities' to equity, which is exactly what the clause does not say.

options.text: Any of its securities listed on a recognised stock exchange in India or abroad
options.explanation: 'Recognised stock exchange' is a defined Indian concept; foreign listings are dealt with separately, including in the Rule 2A carve-outs.

options.text: Its securities offered to the public, whether or not admitted to listing
options.explanation: A public offer is not listing; the definition turns on admission to listing.

options.text: Any of its securities listed on any recognised stock exchange
options.explanation: The clause says 'any of its securities' — equity listing is not required, subject to the carve-outs prescribed under the proviso.

questions.stem: Ranganathan Pipes Private Limited has listed its non-convertible debentures, issued on a private placement basis, on a recognised stock exchange. It has no other listed securities. On the position as on 28 February 2026 it is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(52) proviso with Rule 2A of the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Government, foreign and listed companies →

options.text: A listed company, because 'any of its securities' includes debentures
options.explanation: That is the main limb read without the proviso — the carve-out prescribed under the proviso displaces it here.

options.text: A listed company, and therefore automatically a public company
options.explanation: Two errors: the carve-out applies, and in any event listing does not convert a private company into a public company under s.2(71).

options.text: Not to be considered a listed company, being within the class prescribed under the proviso to s.2(52)
options.explanation: The proviso lets the Central Government prescribe classes that are not to be treated as listed; the Rules currently carve out private companies that have listed only privately-placed non-convertible debt.

options.text: Not a listed company, because a private company can never list any security
options.explanation: A private company may list privately-placed non-convertible debt; the reason for the answer is the prescribed carve-out, not an inability to list.

questions.stem: For the purposes of the definition of 'holding company' in s.2(46), the expression 'company':

options.text: Means only a company incorporated in India under s.2(20)
options.explanation: This ignores the Explanation, which was inserted precisely to widen the term.

options.text: Includes any body corporate, so that a foreign parent can be a holding company
options.explanation: The Explanation to s.2(46) extends 'company' to any body corporate, which is how foreign and other corporate parents are caught.

options.text: Includes a partnership firm carrying on business in India
options.explanation: A firm has no corporate personality and is not a body corporate, so it is outside the extension.

options.text: Includes a body corporate only where the Central Government so notifies
options.explanation: The extension is automatic under the Explanation; no notification is involved.

questions.stem: A company is a subsidiary of another under s.2(87) where the other company:

options.text: Controls the composition of its Board of Directors, OR exercises or controls more than one-half of its total voting power
options.explanation: The two limbs are alternatives; satisfying either one is enough to create the relationship.

options.text: Controls the composition of its Board AND holds more than one-half of its total voting power
options.explanation: This makes the limbs cumulative; the clause uses 'or'.

options.text: Holds more than one-half of its total paid-up share capital
options.explanation: The capital test was replaced by 'total voting power' by the Companies (Amendment) Act 2017.

options.text: Holds at least twenty per cent of its total voting power
options.explanation: 20% is the significant-influence threshold for an ASSOCIATE under s.2(6), not the subsidiary test.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(87)(ii) · Voting power, not capital
questions.stem: Panna Limited has issued 8,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each (one vote per share) and 4,00,000 preference shares of ₹10 each which carry no voting rights except on resolutions directly affecting them. Rewa Limited holds 3,60,000 equity shares and all 4,00,000 preference shares. Panna Limited is:

options.text: An associate of Rewa Limited — 45% of total voting power
options.explanation: Total voting power = 8,00,000 votes (equity only); Rewa controls 3,60,000 = 45%, not more than one-half, so not a subsidiary — but at least 20%, so an associate.

options.text: A subsidiary of Rewa Limited — 63.33% of total paid-up share capital
options.explanation: This uses paid-up capital instead of total voting power; the capital test was dropped from s.2(87)(ii) in 2017.

options.text: A subsidiary of Rewa Limited — 45% of the voting power together with the whole preference capital
options.explanation: Non-voting preference shares add nothing to voting power; they cannot be tacked on to lift 45% over one-half.

options.text: Neither a subsidiary nor an associate of Rewa Limited
options.explanation: This stops at the subsidiary test; 45% is comfortably 'at least twenty per cent' and creates significant influence.

questions.stem: Ojas Ltd has the right, exercisable at its discretion, to appoint 4 of the 9 directors of Pratap Ltd, and holds 30% of Pratap's total voting power. Pratap Ltd is:

options.text: A subsidiary of Ojas Ltd, because Ojas can appoint directors at its discretion
options.explanation: The power must extend to all or a majority of the Board; a right to appoint a minority of directors is not control of its composition.

options.text: An associate of Ojas Ltd — neither limb of s.2(87) is met, but 30% of voting power is significant influence
options.explanation: Board control requires the power to appoint or remove ALL or a MAJORITY of the directors; 4 of 9 is not a majority, and 30% is not more than one-half — so the subsidiary test fails and the associate test succeeds.

options.text: A subsidiary of Ojas Ltd, because the board right and the 30% holding combine
options.explanation: The limbs of s.2(87) are alternatives to be tested separately; they are not aggregated into a composite test.

options.text: Neither a subsidiary nor an associate, because Ojas holds less than one-half of the voting power
options.explanation: This stops at the subsidiary test and never reaches s.2(6), under which 30% is comfortably 'at least twenty per cent'.

questions.stem: Ambika Ltd controls 58% of the total voting power of Bhadra Ltd. Bhadra Ltd controls 51% of Chitra Ltd, and Chitra Ltd controls 70% of Damodar Ltd. Ambika holds no shares directly in Chitra or Damodar. In relation to Ambika Ltd, Chitra Ltd and Damodar Ltd are:

options.text: Chitra an associate (effective holding 29.58%) and Damodar neither
options.explanation: This multiplies 58% × 51% down the chain; s.2(87) never multiplies percentages — control is tested step by step.

options.text: Chitra a subsidiary of Ambika, and Damodar a subsidiary of Chitra only
options.explanation: Explanation (a) does not stop after one step: control by any subsidiary of the holding company counts, and Chitra is such a subsidiary.

options.text: Both associates of Ambika Ltd, since Ambika holds no shares in either
options.explanation: Direct shareholding is not required — the Explanation deems the relationship where control lies with another subsidiary of the holding company.

options.text: Both subsidiaries of Ambika Ltd
options.explanation: Bhadra is Ambika's subsidiary (58%); Chitra is Bhadra's (51%) and so Ambika's by Explanation (a); Damodar is Chitra's (70%) and so Ambika's on the same reasoning.

questions.stem: The restriction on the number of layers of subsidiaries under the proviso to s.2(87), as prescribed by the Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules 2017, is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(87) proviso; Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules 2017

options.text: Not more than two layers, with no exceptions at all
options.explanation: The Rules do carry exceptions, of which the wholly-owned-subsidiary and foreign-acquisition ones are the most examined.

options.text: Not more than three layers, counting the holding company as the first layer
options.explanation: The number is two, and the holding company is not itself a layer — a layer is a subsidiary or subsidiaries.

options.text: Not more than two layers of subsidiaries, with one layer consisting of a wholly-owned subsidiary not counted, and carve-outs for foreign acquisitions and for banking, NBFC, insurance and Government companies
options.explanation: That is the prescribed ceiling and the principal exceptions; 'layer' means a subsidiary or subsidiaries.

options.text: Not more than two layers, but only for listed companies
options.explanation: The Rules apply to prescribed classes of holding companies generally, with named exemptions; listing is not the dividing line.

questions.stem: Godavari Ltd holds 1,50,000 of the 7,50,000 equity shares of Halcyon Ltd, each share carrying one vote. Halcyon has no other voting securities, and there is no agreement between the two companies about Halcyon's business decisions. Halcyon Ltd is:

options.text: Not an associate — significant influence requires MORE than twenty per cent of the total voting power
options.explanation: The Explanation says 'at least twenty per cent'; exactly 20% is inside the definition.

options.text: A subsidiary of Godavari Ltd
options.explanation: A subsidiary needs control of the Board or MORE THAN one-half of the total voting power; 20% is neither.

options.text: An associate of Godavari Ltd — 1,50,000 of 7,50,000 votes is exactly 20%, which is 'at least twenty per cent'
options.explanation: 20.00% meets the significant-influence threshold, and the subsidiary test fails, so s.2(6) applies.

options.text: Not an associate, because there is no agreement about Halcyon's business decisions
options.explanation: The agreement limb is an ALTERNATIVE route to significant influence, not an additional requirement on top of the 20% test.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(41) proviso · Different financial year
questions.stem: A company that is the subsidiary of a company incorporated outside India, and is required to follow a different financial year for consolidation of its accounts outside India, may be allowed a different financial year on an application to:

options.text: The Tribunal (NCLT)
options.explanation: The Tribunal held this jurisdiction under the clause as originally enacted; it was shifted to the Central Government, with a transitional saving for applications already pending.

options.text: The Central Government
options.explanation: As the law stands on 28 February 2026 the application lies to the Central Government; the class of applicants covers a holding, subsidiary or associate company of a foreign company.

options.text: The Registrar of Companies
options.explanation: The Registrar has no power over the financial year; the proviso names a single authority.

options.text: The Board of Directors, by a resolution filed with the Registrar
options.explanation: The financial year is not a matter of internal resolution — the 31 March year-end is mandatory unless the proviso is invoked.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · ss.2(68), 2(71) · Private and public companies
questions.stem: Distinguish between a private company and a public company under the Companies Act 2013. State the counting rules that apply to the 200-member limit, and explain when a private company is treated as a public company. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Private company: articles must (i) restrict the right to transfer shares, (ii) limit members to 200 (not applicable to an OPC), (iii) prohibit any invitation to the public to subscribe for securities
Joint holders of one or more shares are treated as a SINGLE member for the 200-member limb
Excluded from the count: persons in the employment of the company; and persons who were members while in that employment and have continued as members after it ceased

Public company: a company which is not a private company, with such minimum paid-up capital as may be prescribed (nothing currently prescribed; the earlier ₹5 lakh and ₹1 lakh floors were omitted in 2015)

Deeming proviso: a subsidiary of a company which is not a private company is a public company for the purposes of the Act even where it continues to be a private company in its articles — it keeps its articles and its name but loses the private-company relaxations

questions.stem: Define a small company under the Companies Act 2013 as the law stands for the Sept 2026 attempt, and state the companies to which the definition does not apply. Why does the classification matter? (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Small company means a company, other than a public company, satisfying both quantitative limbs — so a public company, listed or not, is never small
Limb (i): paid-up share capital does not exceed the prescribed amount (currently ₹4 crore; the Act caps the prescription at ₹10 crore)

Limb (ii): turnover as per the profit and loss account for the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING financial year does not exceed the prescribed amount (currently ₹40 crore; Act cap ₹100 crore); both limbs are cumulative

Exclusions: (A) a holding company or a subsidiary company; (B) a company registered under section 8; (C) a company or body corporate governed by any special Act — the exclusions apply however small the figures are
Significance: abridged board's report, two board meetings a year instead of four, no mandatory auditor rotation, no cash-flow statement in the financial statements, and lesser penalties

questions.topic: Ch 1 · ss.2(46), 2(87), 2(6) · Holding, subsidiary and associate
questions.stem: When is a company a subsidiary of another company under the Companies Act 2013? Explain, with a short illustration, the position where control is exercised through another subsidiary, and distinguish an associate company. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Subsidiary: a company in which the holding company either (i) controls the composition of the Board of Directors, or (ii) exercises or controls more than one-half of the total VOTING POWER, on its own or with one or more of its subsidiaries — the two limbs are alternatives
Control of Board composition means the power, exercisable at the company's discretion, to appoint or remove all or a majority of the directors

Deemed chain: control exercised by another subsidiary of the holding company counts — if A controls B and B controls C, C is a subsidiary of A; percentages down the chain are never multiplied. Illustration: A holds 58% of B, B holds 51% of C, so both B and C are subsidiaries of A

Layers: prescribed classes of holding companies may not have more than two layers of subsidiaries, with carve-outs including one layer of a wholly-owned subsidiary and the acquisition of a foreign company having more layers under its own law
skeleton.citation: s. 2(87), proviso; Companies (Restriction on Number of Layers) Rules 2017

skeleton.point: Associate: a company in which the other company has significant influence — control of at least 20% of total voting power, or control of or participation in business decisions under an agreement — but which is NOT a subsidiary; includes a joint venture company. Test subsidiary first, associate second

questions.stem: State the doctrine of the corporate veil and explain, with the case anchors, five circumstances in which the courts have lifted it. Mention two statutory instances. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: The rule: on incorporation the company becomes a legal person distinct from its members, with its own property, contracts and liabilities — Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd. Lifting the veil is the exception, not the norm
Fraud or improper conduct: a company formed or used as a device to evade an existing legal obligation is disregarded — Gilford Motor Co v Horne (evasion of a covenant against solicitation)
Sham or facade: a company used as a mask to defeat a contract will not shield the controller — Jones v Lipman (transfer of land to a controlled company to defeat specific performance)
Evasion of tax or revenue: an arrangement whose only purpose is to reduce the controller's tax is looked through — Sir Dinshaw Maneckjee Petit

Enemy character: in wartime the court examines who controls the company — Daimler Co Ltd v Continental Tyre & Rubber Co; and avoidance of statutory/welfare liability — Workmen of Associated Rubber Industry Ltd (subsidiary created to depress a bonus entitlement)

Statutory instances: liability for misstatement in a prospectus; incorporation obtained by furnishing false or incorrect information; liability for fraudulent conduct of business in winding up; and the investigation provisions reaching beneficial owners

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.1 · Application of the Act
questions.stem: State the extent of the Companies Act 2013 and the classes of companies and bodies corporate to which it applies, indicating how the Act interacts with sectoral legislation. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Extent: the Act extends to the whole of India; its provisions were brought into force on such dates as the Central Government notified
Applies to companies incorporated under this Act or under any previous company law — so a company formed under the 1956 Act is governed by the 2013 Act today

Applies to insurance companies, banking companies and companies engaged in the generation or supply of electricity, EXCEPT in so far as the Act's provisions are inconsistent with the Insurance Act 1938 / IRDA Act 1999, the Banking Regulation Act 1949 and the Electricity Act 2003 respectively

Applies to any other company governed by a special Act, subject to the same inconsistency saving; and to such body corporate incorporated by any Act as the Central Government may notify, subject to the exceptions, modifications and adaptations in the notification
Principle: these companies are not outside the Act — the special law prevails only to the extent of the inconsistency, and the rest of the Companies Act continues to apply

questions.stem: Explain the meaning of 'financial year' under the Companies Act 2013, the position of a newly incorporated company, and the circumstances in which a different financial year may be allowed. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Financial year, in relation to any company or body corporate, means the period ending on 31 March every year, in respect of which the financial statement is made up

Where the company or body corporate is incorporated on or after 1 January of a year, its first financial year ends on 31 March of the FOLLOWING year — e.g. incorporation on 12 February 2026 gives a first financial year ending 31 March 2027

Exception: a company or body corporate which is a holding company, a subsidiary or an associate company of a company incorporated OUTSIDE India, and which is required to follow a different financial year for consolidation of its accounts outside India, may apply to be allowed any period as its financial year, whether or not that period is a year

The application lies to the Central Government as the law stands on 28 February 2026 (the jurisdiction having been shifted from the Tribunal), and the relief is available only for the foreign-consolidation reason — not for commercial convenience

questions.topic: Ch 1 · ss.2(87), 2(6), 2(71) · Case: the Sarvodaya group chain
questions.case: Sarvodaya Holdings Limited (an unlisted public company) controls 64% of the total voting power of Trimurti Steel Limited. Trimurti Steel Limited controls 52% of the total voting power of Uttara Alloys Private Limited, whose articles carry all three private-company restrictions. Sarvodaya separately holds 18% of the total voting power of Uttara Alloys and 22% of the total voting power of Varsha Coatings Limited, in which it has no board-appointment rights and no agreement about business decisions. Varsha Coatings has issued 5,00,000 equity shares of ₹10 each with one vote per share and 3,00,000 non-voting preference shares of ₹10 each; Sarvodaya holds 1,10,000 equity shares and 2,40,000 preference shares. All figures are as on 28 February 2026.

questions.stem: The relationship between Sarvodaya Holdings Ltd and Uttara Alloys Private Ltd is that of:

options.text: Holding company and subsidiary, by virtue of the deeming Explanation to s.2(87)
options.explanation: Trimurti is Sarvodaya's subsidiary (64%), and Uttara is Trimurti's (52%); control by a subsidiary of the holding company makes Uttara a subsidiary of Sarvodaya.

options.text: Holding company and associate, the effective holding being 33.28%
options.explanation: This multiplies 64% × 52%; s.2(87) tests control step by step and never multiplies percentages down a chain.

options.text: Holding company and associate, because Sarvodaya's own holding in Uttara is only 18%
options.explanation: The direct 18% is beside the point once the deeming Explanation applies; and s.2(6) excludes a company that is a subsidiary.

options.text: No relationship recognised by the Act, Sarvodaya holding less than one-half of Uttara directly
options.explanation: Direct majority holding is not required — the Explanation catches control exercised through another subsidiary.

questions.stem: Uttara Alloys Private Limited, for the purposes of the Companies Act 2013, is:

options.text: A private company, its articles containing all three restrictions
options.explanation: The deeming proviso overrides the articles expressly.

options.text: A private company, because its immediate holding company Trimurti is limited by shares
options.explanation: The form of the parent's capital is irrelevant; what matters is that the parent is not a PRIVATE company.

options.text: A public company only after it alters its articles and changes its name
options.explanation: The deeming is automatic and requires no alteration of the articles or the name.

options.text: A public company, being a subsidiary of a company which is not a private company
options.explanation: Sarvodaya (and Trimurti, itself deemed public on the same reasoning) is not a private company, so the proviso deems Uttara public despite its articles and its name.

questions.stem: Sarvodaya's holding in Varsha Coatings Limited, expressed as a percentage of TOTAL VOTING POWER, and the resulting relationship, are:

options.text: 43.75% — a subsidiary of Sarvodaya
options.explanation: 43.75% is the share of total PAID-UP CAPITAL (₹11,00,000 + ₹24,00,000 of ₹80,00,000); s.2(87)(ii) uses voting power, and in any case 43.75% is not more than one-half.

options.text: 22% — an associate of Sarvodaya
options.explanation: Total voting power = 5,00,000 votes (equity only, the preference shares carrying no ordinary vote); 1,10,000 ÷ 5,00,000 = 22%, which is not more than one-half but is at least 20% — an associate.

options.text: 22% — neither a subsidiary nor an associate, in the absence of an agreement on business decisions
options.explanation: The agreement limb is an alternative route to significant influence; the 20% voting-power limb is satisfied on its own.

options.text: 13.75% — neither a subsidiary nor an associate
options.explanation: This divides the equity holding by the total number of shares (1,10,000 ÷ 8,00,000) instead of by the total voting power.

questions.stem: If Sarvodaya Holdings Ltd were instead a private company, the effect on Uttara Alloys Private Limited's classification would be:

options.text: Uttara would still be deemed public, the deeming attaching to any subsidiary
options.explanation: The proviso attaches only to a subsidiary of a company that is NOT a private company.

options.text: Uttara would still be deemed public, because Trimurti is a public limited company
options.explanation: This ignores that Trimurti would itself no longer be deemed public if its own parent were private — the chain of deeming must be traced from the top.

options.text: Uttara would remain a private company throughout the chain
options.explanation: With a private company at the top of the chain the proviso is never triggered, so neither Trimurti (if private in its articles) nor Uttara is deemed public.

options.text: Uttara would cease to be a subsidiary of Sarvodaya
options.explanation: The subsidiary relationship under s.2(87) depends on control, not on the class of the parent; only the s.2(71) deeming would change.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · s.2(68) · Case: counting the members of Ratnakar Fabrics
questions.case: Ratnakar Fabrics Private Limited's register of members as on 28 February 2026 records: 132 individuals holding shares in their own names; 15 shareholdings each held jointly by 2 persons; 6 shareholdings each held jointly by 3 persons; 44 current employees of the company who hold shares in their own names; 18 persons who were employees of the company, became members while in that employment, resigned in 2024 and continue to hold their shares; 7 persons who left the company's employment in 2021 and bought shares in 2025; and 260 holders of listed, privately-placed non-convertible debentures. The articles contain all three restrictions required by s.2(68).

questions.stem: The number of members counted for the purposes of s.2(68)(ii) is:

options.explanation: This omits the 7 persons who bought their shares AFTER leaving the company's employment; they do not qualify for the second-proviso exclusion and must be counted.

132 individuals + 15 (each 2-person joint holding is one member) + 6 (each 3-person joint holding is one member) + 7 post-resignation purchasers = 160; current employees and continuing ex-employee members are excluded, and debenture-holders are not members at all.
This counts all 33 joint holders individually instead of treating each joint holding as one member.
This adds the 260 debenture-holders to the count; debenture-holders are creditors, not members.

questions.stem: The 260 debenture-holders affect the company's classification because:

options.text: They push the membership beyond 200 and the company must convert into a public company
options.explanation: Debenture-holders never enter the s.2(68)(ii) count.

options.text: Listing any security makes the company a listed company and therefore a public company
options.explanation: The prescribed carve-out applies, and in any event listing does not convert a private company into a public company under s.2(71).

options.text: A private company may not issue debentures at all
options.explanation: There is no such prohibition; what a private company must not do is invite the PUBLIC to subscribe for its securities.

options.text: They do not — debenture-holders are not members, and a private company that has listed only privately-placed non-convertible debt is within the prescribed carve-out from 'listed company'
options.explanation: Both points hold: the 200-member cap counts members, and Rule 2A keeps such a company outside the listed-company definition.

questions.stem: If the company now admits 45 further individual members, none of them employees and none holding jointly, the position under s.2(68)(ii) will be:

options.text: A breach — 160 + 45 = 205, which exceeds 200
options.explanation: 205 counted members is beyond the statutory cap of 200, so the company cannot admit all 45 while remaining a private company.

options.text: A breach — the register will then show more than 200 names
options.explanation: The test counts members as computed under the provisos, not names on the register.

options.text: No breach — the 44 employee-members create headroom that absorbs the new admissions
options.explanation: The exclusion removes employee-members from the count; it does not create transferable headroom above 200.

options.text: No breach — the cap applies only to members holding equity shares
options.explanation: s.2(68)(ii) speaks of members generally; there is no equity-only qualification.

questions.topic: Ch 1 · ss.2(85), 2(45), 2(42) · Case: classifying four entities
questions.case: Four entities are to be classified as on 28 February 2026. (i) Ashwatha Tools Private Limited: paid-up share capital ₹3,90,00,000; turnover for the immediately preceding financial year ₹39,50,00,000; not a holding or subsidiary company; not registered under s.8; not governed by any special Act. (ii) Bindusar Chemicals Private Limited: paid-up capital ₹80,00,000; preceding-year turnover ₹6,00,00,000; a wholly-owned subsidiary of Bindusar Group Limited. (iii) Chandrika Power Limited: an unlisted public company engaged in the generation of electricity; paid-up capital ₹90,00,000 held as to ₹30,00,000 by the Central Government and ₹22,00,000 by a State Government. (iv) Doronia GmbH: incorporated in Germany, with a branch office in Pune through which it sells and services its equipment in India.

questions.stem: Ashwatha Tools Private Limited is:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(85) with the Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules

options.text: Not a small company — the capital is too close to the prescribed limit to allow a margin
options.explanation: s.2(85) prescribes no margin; the comparator is simply 'does not exceed'.

options.text: Not a small company — the turnover limb must be tested on the current financial year
options.explanation: The clause expressly uses the turnover per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year.

options.text: A small company — ₹3.90 crore does not exceed ₹4 crore and ₹39.50 crore does not exceed ₹40 crore, and no exclusion applies
options.explanation: Both limbs are satisfied on the currently prescribed limits and none of the three exclusions is attracted.

options.text: A small company only if it is also a One Person Company
options.explanation: OPC status is irrelevant to s.2(85); an OPC is neither required for, nor excluded from, small-company status.

questions.stem: Bindusar Chemicals Private Limited and Chandrika Power Limited are, respectively:
questions.sourceRef: s. 2(85), proviso (A) and opening words; s. 2(45); s. 1(4)(d)

options.text: Not a small company (a subsidiary is excluded) and not a small company (a public company can never be small); Chandrika is also a Government company, the Central and State holdings aggregating to 57.78%
options.explanation: Proviso (A) excludes a subsidiary however small its figures; the opening words exclude any public company; and ₹52,00,000 of ₹90,00,000 is 57.78%, which is not less than 51%.

options.text: A small company and a small company, both being within the prescribed capital and turnover limits
options.explanation: This applies only the quantitative limbs and ignores both the subsidiary exclusion and the 'other than a public company' opening.

options.text: Not a small company and a small company — a public company may be small if it is unlisted
options.explanation: The opening words of s.2(85) exclude every public company, listed or not.

options.text: A small company and not a small company — the subsidiary exclusion applies only to a subsidiary of a PUBLIC company
options.explanation: Proviso (A) excludes a holding or subsidiary company without qualifying the class of the other company.

questions.stem: Doronia GmbH is, for the Companies Act 2013:

options.text: A company under s.2(20), because it carries on business in India through a branch
options.explanation: s.2(20) turns on incorporation in India under the Companies Act or a previous company law; a branch does not create it.

options.text: A body corporate and a foreign company, having both a place of business in India and business activity in India
options.explanation: s.2(11) includes a company incorporated outside India, and both limbs of s.2(42) are satisfied by the Pune branch and the selling and servicing carried on through it.

options.text: A foreign company but not a body corporate, s.2(11) covering Indian entities only
options.explanation: s.2(11) expressly includes a company incorporated outside India.

options.text: Neither, unless the Central Government notifies it under s.2(11)
options.explanation: The notification power under s.2(11) is used to exclude bodies corporate from the definition, not to bring them in.
